::: {.lead}
My work as an economist returns to a single question: **how does an emerging economy become a developed one?** It is the defining economic challenge of our time for India and much of the world — and it runs through everything I study, from growth and productivity to trade, monetary policy, and the workings of the labor market.
:::

I am a macroeconomist who works with data and dynamic models. My research spans macroeconomics, international economics, and the structural questions facing emerging economies, with a particular focus on India.

## Current focus: why so many Indians — and most women — are not at work

In recent work with **Aakash Dev**, I ask why nearly half of working-age Indians, and roughly three out of four women, remain outside the labor force. We calibrate a joint household search model to Indian data and find that two forces, usually studied apart, compound one another.

```{=html}
<div class="stat-cards">
  <div class="stat-figure c-coral"><div class="n">3 in 4</div><div class="l">working-age women are not in the labor force</div></div>
  <div class="stat-figure c-teal"><div class="n">~9 hrs</div><div class="l">a day women spend on unpaid household work — men, a fraction</div></div>
  <div class="stat-figure c-blue"><div class="n">45 / 35 / 20</div><div class="l">share of the gap: household burden · market frictions · their interaction</div></div>
</div>

<div class="figure-box">
  <p class="fig-title">Chance of finding a job in any four-month window</p>
  <div class="barchart">
    <div class="bar-row">
      <span class="bar-label">Men</span>
      <span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill c-blue" style="width:96%"></span></span>
      <span class="bar-val c-blue">~24%</span>
    </div>
    <div class="bar-row">
      <span class="bar-label">Women</span>
      <span class="bar-track"><span class="bar-fill c-coral" style="width:28%"></span></span>
      <span class="bar-val c-coral">&lt;7%</span>
    </div>
  </div>
  <p class="cap">A woman's job-finding odds are roughly a third of a man's — so her opportunity cost of working is nearly double, quietly disqualifying most jobs on offer.</p>
</div>
```

The interaction is the point: because the two forces reinforce each other, no single policy can close the gap. This work was the basis of my keynote at the LEO Economics Conference 2026.
